title: Does Every Group Drift Toward Rule by a Few?
h1: Why groups that must decide fast end up ruled by a few, in a new model
question: Is rule by a small elite inevitable in every organisation?
answer: Not in a new model from UC Merced. In simulations published in Royal Society Open Science in November 2026, groups rewarded for fast agreement evolved a few dominant leaders, while groups rewarded for slow deliberation evolved flatter structures. The authors conclude that hierarchy reflects the trade-off between speed and decision quality, not an iron rule.

event.name: Royal Society Open Science publishes "Speed-quality trade-offs shape the structure of decision-making collectives" by Chanuwas Aswamenakul, Tyler Marghetis and Paul E. Smaldino

artefact.text: Phys.org's report, provided by UC Merced, describes the simulated groups, the two scenarios and what the authors take from them.
artefact.label: Read the report

timeline.text: Royal Society Open Science publishes the paper online (volume 13, issue 11, article 252103), by Chanuwas Aswamenakul, Tyler Marghetis and Paul E. Smaldino.

Phys.org carries UC Merced's account of the study under the headline "Do all groups drift toward rule by the few? Not when time is on their side", framing it as a test of Robert Michels's iron law of oligarchy.

mechanism.h: The law says it always happens
mechanism.text: Phys.org sums up Michels's claim: "any organization, however democratic at the start, eventually hands power to an elite." The paper's abstract names the usual reason hierarchy wins: it "provides group-level benefits by speeding up the decision-making process."

mechanism.h: A model with leaders, followers and selection
mechanism.text: The researchers simulated competing groups of 500 members, each with an opinion, that had to reach agreement before acting. Some members were leaders, "persuasive and slow to change their minds"; others were followers, "more easily swayed." Groups that earned higher payoffs passed their mix of leaders and followers to the next generation, so the structure evolved rather than being set.

mechanism.h: Reward speed and a few take over
mechanism.text: In one scenario faster agreement earned bigger payoffs. There, Phys.org reports, "a small number of leaders came to dominate many followers." Persuasive leaders pull a group to agreement quickly, so when speed pays, groups heavy with followers and led by a few win out.

mechanism.h: Reward deliberation and the structure flattens
mechanism.text: In the other scenario slower agreement paid, a stand-in for problems where careful thought matters. Then "groups evolved flatter structures in which most members held similar influence." The pattern held under both unanimous consensus and majority vote. In the abstract's words, groups evolve structures "instead of inevitably becoming centralized and hierarchical."

limits: It is a computer model. The reports we read describe simulations only and do not say the results were tested against real organisations.

It tests the claim that oligarchy is inevitable, not Michels's own causes. Michels pointed to leaders controlling information and the organisation's machinery and wanting to keep their posts; the descriptions we read model persuasive leaders in a decision task, not those causes.

The real-world readings are suggestions. Phys.org reports the authors' ideas about science, cultures and families (that slow, correct results or financial stability may favour flatter norms) as possibilities, not findings.
We could not open the full paper: the publisher's site refused our request. What we say about it comes from its abstract and record at Crossref and from Phys.org's report.

faqs.q: Does this disprove the iron law of oligarchy?
faqs.a: No. It is a model, and it supports half of the law: where fast decisions pay, its groups did end up led by a few. What it questions is the word "iron", the claim that this happens to every organisation whatever it is rewarded for.

faqs.q: What counts as a leader in the model?
faqs.a: A member who is persuasive and slow to change their mind. Followers are easily swayed. The share of each in a group is what evolves.
Not for the main result. Phys.org reports the pattern held whether groups decided by unanimous consensus or by majority vote.

predictions.text: By 31 December 2027 a peer-reviewed study will test the speed-quality account on data from real groups or organisations, not only simulations. This is wrong if no such study, by these authors or others, has been published by then.

actions: If a group you belong to keeps concentrating power, ask what it is rewarded for. On this model, constant pressure to decide fast is what favours a few leaders.
Where decisions must be right more than quick, build in time to deliberate. In the model, that is the condition under which flatter structures won.
When you read that a simulation shows how institutions evolve, check whether it was tested on real ones. This one, as reported, was not.
whyItMatters: The iron law is usually argued as a yes or no: either organisations always fall to a few or they don't. This model turns it into a question with a lever. It ties the drift to oligarchy to how much a group is rewarded for speed, which is something an organisation can see and sometimes change.
